payload.title: Authorised Marriage Celebrants and Who Can Legally Marry You
payload.audience: 30s, couples who are interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, 150k+ AUD budget
payload.reader: An engaged Australian couple in their 30s with a budget of AUD 150k or more, planning a destination wedding, who want to know exactly who has the legal authority to marry them in Australia, how to confirm their celebrant or minister is authorised, whether a friend or family member can do it, and what that authority means if the wedding happens overseas, so the person standing up front makes the marriage legal and the celebration abroad goes ahead without doubt.
payload.goal: Speak with a Wedded Advisor: request a Wedded Concierge consultation at /wonderland-concierge so an advisor can plan the venue, travel, vendors and guest stays for the celebration abroad (the legal ceremony, the celebrant's authority and all paperwork stay with the couple and their authorised celebrant or minister).
payload.angle: Page-one results for 'who can perform a marriage' are mostly US officiant and ordination pages, bare government register pages and individual celebrant blogs selling their services, and none speak to the Australian couple whose celebration is overseas. This guide answers the legal-authority question only as the Attorney-General's Department and the Marriage Act 1961 state it, dated once as at November 2026: the categories of people authorised to solemnise a marriage in Australia, how to check a celebrant on the official register, whether a friend or family member can marry you (and the legal-plus-personal pattern couples use when they cannot), what the authorised celebrant must do (with the NOIM linked, not restated), and religious ceremonies by ministers of recognised denominations, using a Greek Orthodox priest as one example. It then answers the destination question plainly: an Australian celebrant's authority abroad only as official sources state it, and the two paths, a legal ceremony at home then the celebration abroad, or marrying legally under the other country's rules, linking out for the detail. Calm, exact and practical, with no legal advice.
must_include: Intro with a direct answer in the first 100 words: in Australia only a person authorised under the Marriage Act 1961 can solemnise a marriage, with the categories named as AGD states them, dated 'as at November 2026'. Then exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways (who is authorised; check the official register; a friend can only legally marry you if authorised, otherwise a legal ceremony plus a personal one; marrying abroad follows that country's rules or a legal ceremony at home first).

Who can legally marry you: each category of authorised celebrant (for example Commonwealth-registered marriage celebrants, ministers of religion of recognised denominations, state and territory officers, and any other category) only as AGD and the Marriage Act 1961 list them, with [[VERIFY]] markers until sourced. Link /expert-advice/how-to-choose-a-wedding-celebrant for choosing on style and fit.

How to check a celebrant is authorised: the official AGD register of marriage celebrants (and how ministers and state officers are recorded, only as AGD states), what to look for, written as steps. No celebrant names.

Can a friend or family member marry you: the honest legal answer as AGD states it (only if they are, or become, authorised; any route to becoming authorised stated only as AGD describes it, no timeframes or costs unless sourced), and the common pattern of a short legal ceremony with an authorised celebrant plus a personal ceremony led by a friend, framed as an option, not advice.

What your celebrant must do: the legal duties as AGD and the Act state them (receiving the NOIM within the window, checking documents and identity, the required words, witnesses, signing and lodging the paperwork for registration), each with [[VERIFY]] until sourced. Link /expert-advice/notice-of-intended-marriage (draft; link only if live at publish) rather than restating the NOIM, and /expert-advice/what-does-a-celebrant-do-and-do-you-need-one-abroad for the wider role.

Religious ceremonies: ministers of religion of recognised denominations can solemnise marriages in Australia, as AGD states; the Greek Orthodox priest as one example only, linking /destination-weddings/greek-orthodox-wedding (draft; link only if live at publish); no church names, fees or doctrine beyond official sources.

Marrying abroad (the differentiator): whether an Australian celebrant's authority applies outside Australia, stated only as AGD, DFAT or Smartraveller state it; Option A, a legal ceremony in Australia then the celebration abroad; Option B, marrying legally under the other country's rules (link /expert-advice/what-is-a-certificate-of-no-impediment-and-who-issues-it, /expert-advice/what-is-an-apostille-and-does-my-paperwork-need-one, /expert-advice/should-you-marry-legally-abroad-or-have-a-symbolic-ceremony, /expert-advice/do-you-have-to-register-an-overseas-marriage-at-home, /expert-advice/overseas-marriage-certificate). This section carries the ONLY Advisor line in the body (brand-facts claims only: venue, travel, vendors and guests, never legal paperwork or providing a celebrant for legal purposes) plus the /wonderland-concierge link (anchor names 'Wedded Concierge').

FAQ (4 to 6): Who can legally perform a marriage in Australia? How do I check my celebrant is authorised? Can a friend marry us? Can a minister of religion marry us? Can an Australian celebrant marry us overseas? Do we need a legal ceremony in Australia if we marry abroad? Each answer from the same sources as the body.

Close: the one Advisor line from brand-facts.md (never the definition line or its closing phrase). Links /wonderland-concierge (Wedded Concierge) and /magazine as the magnet. UTMs utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=who-can-perform-a-marriage&utm_content=primary|secondary|magnet|closing on /wonderland-concierge and /magazine only.
avoid: Any legal statement not from AGD, the Marriage Act 1961 or another official Australian government source (DFAT, Smartraveller) read live; undated legal claims; legal advice ('check with your celebrant or the authorities' instead).
US or other-country officiant rules (online ordination, judges, ship captains) unless an official Australian source addresses them.
Any price, fee or amount, including celebrant fees, registration or training costs; 'free'.
Rules for marrying in a specific foreign country beyond what an official source states; link out rather than restate.
Celebrant, minister, church or vendor names; 'best' or ranking language; transfers, drive or flight times.
Anything implying the Wedded Advisor or Wedded Concierge provides or arranges a celebrant for legal purposes, or helps with the NOIM, documents, the CNI or any legal paperwork.

Wedded Privileges; Advisor claims beyond brand-facts.md; more than one Advisor line in the body besides the close; the Advisor definition line and the phrase 'last dance'; 'Wonderland Concierge' as anchor text.
Restating the NOIM process, celebrant-choosing advice or the celebrant's wider role, which their own pages own.
Research talk in copy ('we could not confirm', 'according to our research'); per-line source credits; hedge stacking.
Competitor wedding sites, celebrant blogs, directories or Wikipedia as sources; competitor wording or images.
Clichés, exclamation marks, keywords pasted in headings, em dashes, US spelling.
